strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework using statistical physics tools (MSRDJ formalism, VGA) with sound self-averaging argument and CLT justification for Gaussianity
Novel unification of Bayesian inference, gradient flow, and Langevin dynamics in single theoretical framework
Parsimonious description using two order parameters (R̄ and C̄), more interpretable than prior work requiring auxiliary fields
Insightful mechanistic explanation of early stopping via bias-variance decomposition and analysis of regularization effects on variance vs. bias timescales
Strong experimental validation across Figures 1-4 with systematic parameter variation (β, gβ, γ) and adequate disorder averaging (10⁵ realizations)
Elegant mathematical development reducing high-dimensional dynamics to interpretable lower-dimensional order parameters with memory kernel mediating mode coupling
Thorough technical exposition with detailed appendices (A-E) providing complete derivations from disorder averaging to effective equations
weaknesses: Severely limited applicability: restricted to linear/kernel regression without feature learning; connection to real neural networks is indirect and unproven

Power-law eigenvalue spectrum assumed as input (Eq. 9) rather than derived from architecture or data; claim to 'explain' neural scaling laws (p. 1) is overstated—theory explains dynamics *given* power laws, not their origin
Large-N asymptotic analysis throughout with no finite-size corrections or breakdown analysis; unclear how accurate theory is for N≈100-1000 tested in simulations
Strong assumptions (Gaussian features, orthogonality relation) with limited robustness analysis; no exploration of failures under non-Gaussian or correlated features
Incomplete quantitative characterization of early stopping: no analytical formula for optimal stopping time t_opt(β, gβ, γ, P, N) or explicit time-dependent scaling laws L_test(t)
Experiments limited to synthetic data with modest system sizes; main power-law exponent tested only at γ=3/2; no real-data validation or regime where theory fails
Presentation density with heavy notation (bars, tildes, hats) and key intuitions (memory kernel as Onsager term) relegated to Discussion; physical interpretation could precede mathematics

strengths: Rigorous and comprehensive dynamical mean-field theory using MSRDJ formalism and variational Gaussian approximation, properly handling disorder averaging and recovering known limits as validation
Successfully unifies multiple learning regimes (Bayesian inference, gradient flow, Langevin dynamics) under a single theoretical framework with interpretable order parameters (R, C, C̃)

Novel mechanistic insights including: memory kernel mediating mode coupling and learning slowdown, mode decoupling conditional on order parameters, bias-variance decomposition explaining early stopping, and the striking result that optimal stopping time is independent of P and N
Thorough experimental validation with good theory-simulation agreement across multiple parameter regimes and extensions (label noise, different regularization strengths)

Exceptionally detailed mathematical exposition in appendices (A-C) that makes derivations transparent and reproducible, with careful identification of order parameters and justification for dropping subleading terms
weaknesses: Severely restricted scope: limited entirely to linear kernel regression. No results for feature learning or nonlinear networks beyond brief speculative discussion. Applicability to understanding real neural networks remains unclear, undermining stated motivation

Critical unjustified assumptions: (1) Gaussian features ψᵢ~N(0,ηᵢδᵢⱼ)—robustness to non-Gaussian or structured kernels unknown; (2) specific power-law decay ηᵢ=η₁i^{-1-γ}—no guidance on identifying α from data; (3) identical student-teacher features—artificial relative to prior work on down-projected settings; (4) VGA exactness only as N→∞—finite-N convergence rates not characterized

Presentation issues: extremely dense notation with scattered key results across appendices limits accessibility. Figures 2b and 3 are difficult to parse. The intuitive interpretation of scaling laws (Section 5) lacks intermediate explanation connecting microscopic dynamics to macroscopic phenomena

Limited technical novelty in some components: scaling laws (Eqs. 34-37) recover Bordelon et al. (2024) as acknowledged; static limit recovers Canatar et al. (2021) exactly; label noise extension is straightforward application of framework

Approximations lack rigor: (1) OUP approximation (replacing Q with ⟨Q⟩) provides lower bound on bias decay with unanalyzed tightness; (2) finite-size corrections O(N^{-α}) can be substantial (visible in figures) but not thoroughly analyzed; (3) self-averaging property stated but not proven with finite-N rates

Limited experimental scope and practical utility: modest system sizes (N,P≤1000), only one or two power-law exponents tested, visible theory-simulation discrepancies at intermediate times, no demonstration on realistic datasets or guidance on estimating α from data, unclear how to apply results for algorithm design

Missing critical analyses: no robustness study for violations of Gaussian assumption, no characterization of convergence to mean-field limit, no discussion of phase transitions when Pηᵢ~1/gβ, limited treatment of how results change with input correlations or non-isotropic features

strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework using MSRDJ formalism and variational Gaussian approximation with careful large-N analysis
Successful unification of multiple training regimes (Bayesian inference, gradient flow, Langevin dynamics) under single theoretical framework
Excellent quantitative agreement between theory and simulations across diverse regimes (Figures 1-5)
Multiple novel physical insights: spectral bias as dynamic phenomenon, disorder-induced memory kernel slowing learning, emergent noise correlations, independence of optimal stopping time from P and N
Effective reduction of high-dimensional dynamics to interpretable lower-dimensional order parameters
Comprehensive treatment including extensions to label noise and sketches toward nonlinear settings
Well-organized presentation with detailed derivations enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Restriction to linearized kernel regression and linear regression limits applicability; connection to actual neural network training through NTK is indirect
Strong assumptions on data: Gaussian feature distribution, orthogonal features with power-law decay may not generalize to broader settings
Finite-size corrections are non-negligible (Figure 4 shows N^{-α} terms), limiting practical applicability for realistic system sizes
VGA is exact only in N→∞ limit without quantified convergence analysis; Ornstein-Uhlenbeck approximation impacts not fully explored
Early stopping time result (t* independent of P, N) holds only to leading order; robustness to assumption violations not thoroughly discussed
Nonlinear extensions incomplete: Section J left for future work, no discussion of activation function dependence
Limited practical guidance: optimal stopping formula elegant but hyperparameter selection strategy unclear
Theory-experiment differences not quantified (e.g., errors as function of N, P)
Comparative advantages over closely related work (Bordelon et al. 2024) remain somewhat subtle; specific novelty could be better highlighted
